summary: Describes the Extensible Provisioning Protocol, an XML client-server protocol for provisioning and managing objects in a shared central repository, such as a domain registry. It defines generic operations and an extensible framework. It is a draft standard, replaced by RFC 5730.

eli5.summary: Domain name companies keep their records in a central book. EPP is the shared language for writing in that book.

questions: how do registrars talk to registries
what is the domain name provisioning protocol
subtitle: The standard XML protocol for domain registrars to manage objects in central registries.

tldr.problem: Domain registrars and registries needed a standard way to communicate about managing domain names, name servers, and contacts in a shared central repository.
tldr.mechanism: EPP is a stateful XML client-server protocol that defines commands for session management, queries, and object modifications, with an extensible framework to support different object types.
tldr.outcome: EPP became the standard protocol for registrar-registry communication and is widely used in domain name systems worldwide.

today: RFC 4930 is a Draft Standard. It was superseded by RFC 5730 in August 2009, which provides further clarifications and improvements. EPP remains the standard protocol for registrar-registry communication, and modern implementations use RFC 5730.

sections.title: What is EPP
sections.content:
RFC 4930 specifies the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP), an XML-based client-server protocol for managing objects in a shared central repository. The protocol was designed to allow multiple service providers (registrars) to interact with a central repository (registry) using a standardized language.

EPP is stateful, meaning a client establishes a session with a server and maintains that connection for multiple commands. The protocol is built on XML and uses a command-response model: a client sends a command, and the server responds with the results. All EPP commands are atomic, meaning they either succeed completely or fail completely; partial success is not allowed.
sections.eli5: EPP is like a conversation between a registrar and a registry. They log in, have a chat where the registrar asks questions or makes changes, and then log out. Each message follows strict rules so there is no confusion.

sections.title: Protocol Architecture and Structure
sections.content:
EPP divides its commands into three categories. Session management commands are used to establish and end sessions: the <login> command authenticates the client and negotiates protocol options, while the <logout> command ends the session cleanly.

Query commands allow read-only operations: <check> tests whether an object can be provisioned, <info> retrieves information about an existing object, <poll> retrieves queued messages from the server, and <transfer> in query mode checks the status of transfer requests.

Transform commands modify objects: <create> adds a new object, <delete> removes one, <renew> extends its validity period, <transfer> handles changes in sponsorship, and <update> modifies existing object attributes.
sections.eli5: EPP commands are organized into three types: logging in and out, asking questions, and making changes. This keeps the protocol organized and easy to understand.

sections.title: Extension Framework
sections.content:
A key design feature of EPP is its extensibility. The protocol does not define specific objects like domain names or contacts; instead, it provides a framework for defining them. Objects are identified using XML namespaces, and each object mapping is defined in a separate specification document.

EPP supports three levels of extensions. Protocol extensions add new features at the protocol level using an <extension> element. Object extensions define how specific objects are managed using object-specific child elements and schemas. Command-response extensions allow additional elements in specific commands or responses for server-specific functionality.

This design makes EPP flexible: new object types can be added without modifying the base protocol. For example, RFC 5731 defines domain name handling, RFC 5732 defines contact handling, and other documents define name servers and other objects.
sections.eli5: EPP is like a template for communication. The template is the same for everyone, but different organizations can fill it in with their own object types. This means you can use EPP for domains, contacts, or anything else without changing the basic rules.

sections.title: Message Exchange and Operations
sections.content:
A session begins when a client connects and the server responds with a <greeting> containing the server's name, supported protocol versions, available object types, and data collection policies. The client then sends a <login> command with credentials and options, selecting which objects it wishes to manage.

After authentication, the client exchanges commands with the server. The server processes each command in the order received and sends a response. Each response includes a result code, a human-readable message, and optionally response data. Result codes are four-digit numbers: codes starting with 1 indicate success, codes starting with 2 indicate failure. The second digit indicates the category (syntax, implementation, security, data management, server system, or connection management).

EPP includes a message queue mechanism: the server can queue notifications for the client and deliver them via the <poll> command. This allows the server to notify a client about asynchronous events, such as the completion of an offline action or a transfer request from another registrar.
sections.eli5: A typical EPP session is like a phone call: greetings, identification, requests and answers, then goodbye. The server uses a code system to say whether each request worked or had a problem.

sections.title: Transport and Security Considerations
sections.content:
EPP is transport-agnostic, meaning it can be carried over multiple transport protocols. However, the RFC specifies that the transport mapping must preserve command order, ensure reliability, address the stateful nature of the protocol, frame data units, and implement congestion avoidance. Transport mappings are specified in separate documents; for example, EPP over TCP is defined in RFC 3734.

EPP is designed to work with lower-layer security protocols such as TLS. The protocol itself does not define authentication mechanisms beyond the login command; more robust security is expected to be provided at the transport layer. Similarly, the protocol does not specify how to manage the relationship between sessions and physical connections, leaving that to the transport mapping.

Pipelining (sending multiple commands without waiting for responses) is allowed but optional, and the RFC notes that implementations must handle the ordering and independence of pipelined commands carefully.
sections.eli5: EPP does not care how the messages travel over the network, whether by TCP, SMTP, or other means. Security is handled by the lower layer underneath EPP, like using encryption. This makes EPP flexible but requires the lower layers to do their job.

sections.title: Status and Standardization
sections.content: RFC 4930 obsoletes RFC 3730, which was the original EPP specification from 1999. The updates in RFC 4930 include clarifications and improvements based on operational experience. RFC 4930 was itself obsoleted by RFC 5730 in May 2007, which provided further updates and clarifications. Today, RFC 5730 is the standard EPP protocol specification.
sections.eli5: This RFC was an update to an earlier version of the same protocol. A newer version (RFC 5730) has since replaced it. If you are using EPP today, you are probably using RFC 5730.
